chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Basir, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about their actions, and he said to me, 'O Abu Muhammad, no and no, a short time with a pen. Indeed, one of you does not gain anything from their worldly wealth except that they gain the like of it from his religion,' or 'until they gain from his religion the like of it.' The doubt is from Ibn Abi Umayr.

key_terms.أَعْمَالِهِمْ: Their actions/deeds (referring to the Imams or the wealthy)
key_terms.الْوَهْمُ: The doubt/uncertainty (referring to the narrator's uncertainty in the chain)
key_terms.بِقَلَمٍ: With a pen (metaphor for recording or brief duration/accounting)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual cost of consuming the wealth of the Imams or the righteous?
ai.summary: In the chapter on trade (*al-Makasib*), Imam al-Baqir (AS) elucidates the spiritual economy of *khums* and Imamate wealth, warning that worldly gain from the Imam's assets incurs a proportional deduction from one's religious merit (*din*). This narration underscores the principle of *muqabalah* (exchange), where material benefit is balanced by spiritual accountability, a concept central to Shia jurisprudence regarding the distribution of Imamate funds. It serves as a cautionary reminder that accessing the Imam's wealth is not merely a financial transaction but a covenant with spiritual consequences.
